張燮

同考試官訓導俞批：題以禮樂立說，前後貫串，渾然無斧鑿痕，作手也。
同考試官教諭魏批：文足以發題意，他日有位，必能推所學以愛人者。
考試官教諭姜批：親切有味。
考試官教諭徐批：文有曲折斡旋，可美。

惟在上知所學，則於下知所愛。夫愛人本於學道也，然則君子之於道，可不知所學哉？昔子游以禮樂治武城，因夫子莞爾之戲，而質以平日所聞之言如此。意謂君子任民社之寄，有家國之責，固不可以不學，學不可以不致於道。必也格物致知，而於事物之理無不明；篤志力行，而於事物之理無不體。如道不外乎禮也，而禮有
translation_en:
First Session
Four Books
“When the gentleman studies the Way, he loves others”
Zhang Xie

Comment by Associate Examiner Yu, Assistant Instructor: The essay develops its argument through rites and music, maintaining coherence throughout. It forms a seamless whole, without a trace of forced workmanship: this is an accomplished writer.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wei, Instructor: The composition fully brings out the meaning of the topic. If the author holds office in the future, he will surely be able to extend what he has learned to loving others.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Instructor: Closely attuned to the subject and rich in meaning.

Comment by Examiner Xu, Instructor: The composition moves deftly through its turns and developments. It merits praise.

Only when those above know what they should learn will they know whom they should love below. Loving others is rooted in studying the Way. How, then, can the gentleman fail to know what he should learn concerning the Way? Formerly, Ziyou governed Wucheng through rites and music. When the Master smiled and made a jest, Ziyou responded by citing words he had previously heard from him, to this effect. The meaning is that the gentleman, entrusted with the people and the altars of the soil, bears responsibility for the ruling house and the state. He certainly cannot dispense with learning, and his learning must reach the Way. He must investigate things and extend his knowledge, leaving no principle of affairs and things uncomprehended; he must make his resolve firm and earnestly put it into practice, leaving no principle of affairs and things unembodied. For example, the Way does not lie outside the rites, and the rites have…

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
三千三百之詳君子則博而約之以究其至中
之歸道不外乎樂也而樂有五聲六律之變君
子則講而習之以探其至和之蘊由是持循也
久而鄙詐慢易之心釋涵養也熟而易直子諒
之心生以之治人則廓然大公而無非仁愛之
周流以之臨民則怡然樂易而無非慈愛之浹
洽如民未協乎中吾所憫也於是節之以禮使
其薰陶漸染而皆趨於至中之域民未得其和
吾不忍也於是和之以樂使其優游厭飫而皆
===
囿於至和之化夫君子學道之功至於如此曾
謂為治者可不以禮樂為教哉嗟夫天下一道
也君子學之則愛人小人學之則易使皆不可
以不學也彼武城雖小將為君子焉將為小人
焉使不以禮樂為教則上虐其下下凌其上不
可一日而為治矣故子游以昔日之所聞為今
日之所教誠知所先務矣夫子驟聞而深喜之
不亦宜乎
知斯三者則知所以脩身
punctuated:
三千三百之詳，君子則博而約之，以究其至中之歸。道不外乎樂也，而樂有五聲六律之變，君子則講而習之，以探其至和之蘊。由是持循也久，而鄙詐慢易之心釋；涵養也熟，而易直子諒之心生。以之治人，則廓然大公，而無非仁愛之周流；以之臨民，則怡然樂易，而無非慈愛之浹洽。如民未協乎中，吾所憫也，於是節之以禮，使其薰陶漸染，而皆趨於至中之域；民未得其和，吾不忍也，於是和之以樂，使其優游厭飫，而皆囿於至和之化。夫君子學道之功至於如此，曾謂為治者可不以禮樂為教哉？嗟夫！天下一道也，君子學之則愛人，小人學之則易使，皆不可以不學也。彼武城雖小，將為君子焉，將為小人焉，使不以禮樂為教，則上虐其下，下凌其上，不可一日而為治矣。故子游以昔日之所聞，為今日之所教，誠知所先務矣。夫子驟聞而深喜之，不亦宜乎？

知斯三者，則知所以脩身。
translation_en:
…the detailed provisions of its three thousand and three hundred rules. The gentleman studies them broadly and draws them together into their essentials, thereby investigating their ultimate convergence upon perfect balance. The Way does not lie outside music; music has the variations of the five tones and six pitch standards. The gentleman studies and practices these to explore the depths of perfect harmony. Through prolonged adherence to these practices, thoughts of baseness, deceit, arrogance, and disrespect dissolve; as self-cultivation matures, a disposition of gentleness, uprightness, kindness, and trustworthiness arises. When he applies this to governing others, he is expansive and wholly impartial, and benevolent love circulates everywhere. When he applies it to overseeing the people, he is cheerful and gracious, and compassionate love permeates all.

If the people have not attained balance, this arouses his compassion. He therefore regulates them through ritual, allowing its gradual influence to imbue them until all approach the realm of perfect balance. If the people have not attained harmony, he cannot bear it. He therefore harmonizes them through music, allowing them to dwell at ease in it and absorb it fully until all are encompassed by the transforming influence of perfect harmony. When the gentleman’s achievement in learning the Way reaches such a point, could anyone maintain that those who govern may dispense with ritual and music as instruments of instruction?

Ah! There is one Way throughout the world. When gentlemen learn it, they love others; when common people learn it, they become easy to direct. Neither can dispense with learning it. Though Wucheng is small, there will be gentlemen there and there will be common people. If ritual and music are not used to teach them, those above will oppress those below, and those below will affront those above: orderly government could not be sustained for even a day. Thus Ziyou made what he had heard in former days the basis of his teaching today. He truly understood what must receive priority. Was it not fitting that the Master, upon suddenly hearing this, was deeply pleased?

“To know these three things is to know how to cultivate oneself.”

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
戴大賓
同考試官教諭李批題中二知字頗為有
力而所以脩身處亦難發揮惟此作剖析明白
而詞理俱到故録之
同考試官學正王批題甚冠冕而佳作絶
少求其辭理明暢快人心目者僅見此篇允宜前列
考試官教諭姜批平正通達有
國初渾厚氣味
考試官教諭徐批可謂文章爾雅者
===
能知所以入乎德則知所以治乎巳盖治巳本
乎道而行道本乎德也能知入德之事則所以
行道而脩身者豈外是哉中庸引夫子告哀公
之言以明道之費隱及此謂夫為政之本固在
於身而脩身之道則由於德德豈易及哉是故
知雖有未及也能知自是之為愚而惟學之是
好則足以破愚而近乎知焉仁雖有未及也能
知徇欲之為私而惟行之是力則足以忘私而
近乎仁焉勇雖有未及也能知甘為人下之為
punctuated:
戴大賓

同考試官教諭李批：題中二知字頗為有力，而所以脩身處亦難發揮。惟此作剖析明白，而詞理俱到，故録之。

同考試官學正王批：題甚冠冕，而佳作絶少。求其辭理明暢、快人心目者，僅見此篇，允宜前列。

考試官教諭姜批：平正通達，有國初渾厚氣味。

考試官教諭徐批：可謂文章爾雅者。

能知所以入乎德，則知所以治乎巳。盖治巳本乎道，而行道本乎德也。能知入德之事，則所以行道而脩身者，豈外是哉？《中庸》引夫子告哀公之言，以明道之費隱，及此謂夫為政之本固在於身，而脩身之道則由於德。德豈易及哉？是故知雖有未及也，能知自是之為愚，而惟學之是好，則足以破愚而近乎知焉；仁雖有未及也，能知徇欲之為私，而惟行之是力，則足以忘私而近乎仁焉；勇雖有未及也，能知甘為人下之為
translation_en:
Dai Dabin

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Instructor: The two occurrences of “know” in the topic carry considerable force, while the passage concerning the means of cultivating oneself is also difficult to expound. This composition alone analyzes the matter clearly and achieves excellence in both expression and reasoning; hence its inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, School Instructor: The topic is most dignified, yet fine compositions are exceedingly rare. In seeking one whose expression and reasoning are lucid and fluent, delighting the reader’s mind and eye, I have found only this piece. It certainly deserves a place among the foremost.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Instructor: Balanced, correct, lucid, and comprehensive, it has the substantial, generous spirit of the dynasty’s early years.

Comment by Examiner Xu, Instructor: This may be called a composition of refined elegance.

If one can know the means of entering into virtue, one knows the means of governing oneself. For governing oneself is rooted in the Way, while practicing the Way is rooted in virtue. If one can understand the work of entering into virtue, how could the means of practicing the Way and cultivating oneself lie outside this? The Doctrine of the Mean quotes the Master’s words to Duke Ai to illuminate the Way’s extensive manifestations and hidden subtlety. At this point, it explains that the foundation of government assuredly lies in oneself, while the way to cultivate oneself proceeds from virtue. Yet how could virtue be easy to attain? Thus, although one may not yet have attained wisdom, if one can recognize that considering oneself always right is foolishness, and devote oneself solely to a love of learning, this suffices to overcome foolishness and approach wisdom. Although one may not yet have attained benevolence, if one can recognize that indulging one’s desires is selfishness, and devote one’s efforts solely to practice, this suffices to forget selfishness and approach benevolence. Although one may not yet have attained courage, if one can recognize that being content to remain inferior to others is …

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
懦而恥之則其學也不厭其行也不倦亦足以
起懦而近乎勇焉夫知三近以入德則知行道
以脩身彼知所以知達道也道有未知則身有
未脩能知好學近乎知則必以此知而知此道
心與道而相涵矣非知所以脩身乎仁所以體
達道也道有未體則身有未脩能知力行近乎
仁則必以此仁而體此道身與道而相安矣又
非知所以脩身乎勇所以強達道也使道有餒
焉則身亦不可得而脩矣能知知恥近乎勇則
===
必以此勇而強此道愚可進於明柔可進於強
不謂之脩身而何哉是則欲盡脩身之道當先
入德之事君子欲脩其身者可不知所務歟大
抵人君一身家國天下之本也不脩其身則取
舍不明而無以為取人之則欲家國天下之治
難矣故夫子於哀公之問既曰脩身以道脩道
以仁又曰君子不可以不脩身下文又以脩身
為九經之首一篇之中言之不一而足無非欲
其脩身以立家國天下之本耳哀公果能體而
punctuated: 懦而恥之，則其學也不厭，其行也不倦，亦足以起懦而近乎勇焉。夫知三近以入德，則知行道以脩身。彼知，所以知達道也；道有未知，則身有未脩。能知好學近乎知，則必以此知而知此道，心與道而相涵矣，非知所以脩身乎？仁，所以體達道也；道有未體，則身有未脩。能知力行近乎仁，則必以此仁而體此道，身與道而相安矣，又非知所以脩身乎？勇，所以強達道也；使道有餒焉，則身亦不可得而脩矣。能知知恥近乎勇，則必以此勇而強此道，愚可進於明，柔可進於強，不謂之脩身而何哉？是則欲盡脩身之道，當先入德之事。君子欲脩其身者，可不知所務歟？大抵人君一身，家國天下之本也。不脩其身，則取舍不明，而無以為取人之則，欲家國天下之治，難矣。故夫子於哀公之問，既曰「脩身以道，脩道以仁」，又曰「君子不可以不脩身」，下文又以脩身為九經之首。一篇之中，言之不一而足，無非欲其脩身以立家國天下之本耳。哀公果能體而
translation_en:
…cowardice and feel ashamed of it, then they will be tireless in learning and unflagging in practice. This, too, is sufficient to rouse them from cowardice and bring them close to courage. Knowing these three approaches to virtue, one knows how to practice the Way and cultivate oneself. Wisdom is that by which one understands the universally applicable Way. Where the Way remains unknown, self-cultivation remains incomplete. If one knows that loving learning brings one close to wisdom, one will surely use this wisdom to understand the Way, so that mind and Way mutually inform one another. Is this not knowing how to cultivate oneself? Benevolence is that by which one embodies the universally applicable Way. Where the Way has not been embodied, self-cultivation remains incomplete. If one knows that earnest practice brings one close to benevolence, one will surely use this benevolence to embody the Way, so that one’s person and the Way rest in harmony with each other. Is this not also knowing how to cultivate oneself? Courage is that by which one steadfastly upholds the universally applicable Way. If one falters in pursuing the Way, self-cultivation likewise becomes impossible. If one knows that knowing shame brings one close to courage, one will surely use this courage to uphold the Way steadfastly. The foolish can advance toward understanding, and the weak toward strength. What could this be called but self-cultivation? Thus, to fulfill the way of self-cultivation, one must begin with the means of entering into virtue. Can a gentleman wishing to cultivate himself fail to know where to direct his efforts?

Broadly speaking, the ruler’s own person is the foundation of the family, the state, and all under Heaven. If he does not cultivate himself, he cannot clearly discern what to accept and reject, and will have no standard for selecting men for office. It will then be difficult to secure good order in the family, the state, and all under Heaven. Thus, in answering Duke Ai’s question, Confucius said both, “Cultivate oneself through the Way, and cultivate the Way through benevolence,” and “The gentleman must cultivate himself.” Further on, he also placed self-cultivation first among the nine guiding principles. Within a single chapter, he spoke of it repeatedly, solely because he wished the ruler to cultivate himself and thereby establish the foundation of the family, the state, and all under Heaven. If Duke Ai could truly embody it and…

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
行之則有君有臣而政無不舉東魯其西周矣
惜乎其不能也噫
人皆有所不忍達之於其所忍仁也人皆
有所不為達之於其所為義也人能充無
欲害人之心而仁不可勝用也人能充無
穿窬之心而義不可勝用也
陳艮山
同考試官教諭杜批達充二字此題關鍵
場中知者絕少此作會註成文而理自見錄之
===
同考試官教諭羅批意達而詞不費稠
人中僅見此篇
考試官教諭姜批融會傳註成文冲
淡中有不盡之味
考試官教諭徐批簡潔
推仁義之端而用以行充仁義之量而用以廣
夫仁義之心本然全具也誠能推而充之豈有
不足於用哉昔孟子之意謂夫仁義之性雖出
於天而擴充之功則在於人是故惻隱之心仁
punctuated:
行之，則有君有臣，而政無不舉，東魯其西周矣。惜乎其不能也！噫！

人皆有所不忍，達之於其所忍，仁也。人皆有所不為，達之於其所為，義也。人能充無欲害人之心，而仁不可勝用也。人能充無穿窬之心，而義不可勝用也。

陳艮山

同考試官教諭杜批：「達、充二字，此題關鍵，場中知者絕少。此作會註成文，而理自見，錄之。」

同考試官教諭羅批：「意達而詞不費，稠人中僅見此篇。」

考試官教諭姜批：「融會傳註成文，冲淡中有不盡之味。」

考試官教諭徐批：「簡潔。」

推仁義之端，而用以行；充仁義之量，而用以廣。夫仁義之心，本然全具也。誠能推而充之，豈有不足於用哉？昔孟子之意，謂夫仁義之性雖出於天，而擴充之功則在於人。是故惻隱之心，仁
translation_en:
…put it into practice, then ruler and ministers would each fulfill their roles, and every affair of government would be carried out. Lu in the east would become another Western Zhou. What a pity that he could not do so! Alas!

“Everyone has things he cannot bear to do; extending this feeling to what he can bear to do is benevolence. Everyone has things he will not do; extending this restraint to what he will do is righteousness. If a person can fully develop the heart that has no wish to harm others, his benevolence will be inexhaustible in its application. If a person can fully develop the heart that has no wish to bore through walls or climb over them to steal, his righteousness will be inexhaustible in its application.”

Chen Genshan 陳艮山

Comment by Associate Examiner Du, Instructor: “The two words ‘extend’ and ‘fully develop’ are the key to this topic. Very few in the examination hall understood this. This composition integrates the commentaries into its writing, so that the principle becomes evident of itself. I have selected it for inclusion.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Luo, Instructor: “The meaning is clearly conveyed without wasting words. Among the multitude of candidates, this is the only such piece I have seen.”

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Instructor: “The composition thoroughly integrates the exegetical commentaries. Within its unadorned simplicity lies an inexhaustible savor.”

Comment by Examiner Xu, Instructor: “Concise and clear.”

Extend the beginnings of benevolence and righteousness, and thereby put them into practice; develop their full capacity, and thereby broaden their application. The heart of benevolence and righteousness is, in its original condition, complete in every respect. If one can truly extend and fully develop it, how could it ever be insufficient in application? What Mencius meant was that, although the nature endowed with benevolence and righteousness comes from Heaven, the work of extending and fully developing it rests with human beings. Thus, the heart of compassion is benevolence’s…

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
之端也人皆有之故莫不有所不忍焉然氣拘
物蔽有不忍於此而或忍於彼者但推所不忍
以達於所忍則惻隱之心無所壅蔽而無非仁
矣羞惡之心義之端也人皆有之故莫不有所
不爲焉然知誘物化有不爲於此而或爲於彼
者但推所不爲以達於所爲則羞惡之心無所
間隔而無非義矣夫有所不忍即無欲害人之
心也人能推所不忍以達於所忍而至於事事
皆不忍焉則能充其無欲害人之心而愛無不
===
周矣仁之用寧有既乎有所不爲即無穿窬之
心也人能推所不爲以達於所爲而至于事事
皆不爲焉則能滿其無穿窬之心而行無不宜
矣義之用寧有窮乎是則仁義之心人所固有
茍有之而不能推推之而不能充而以爲未嘗
有仁義焉者是豈人之本心哉大抵人有是心
莫非全體雖包括天地兼利萬物亦其能事也
然有所蔽而不能盡乎此心之量則恩及禽獸
而功不至于百姓耻受嘑蹴而義不辨乎萬鍾
punctuated: 之端也，人皆有之，故莫不有所不忍焉。然氣拘物蔽，有不忍於此而或忍於彼者。但推所不忍，以達於所忍，則惻隱之心無所壅蔽，而無非仁矣。羞惡之心，義之端也，人皆有之，故莫不有所不爲焉。然知誘物化，有不爲於此而或爲於彼者。但推所不爲，以達於所爲，則羞惡之心無所間隔，而無非義矣。夫有所不忍，即無欲害人之心也。人能推所不忍，以達於所忍，而至於事事皆不忍焉，則能充其無欲害人之心，而愛無不周矣。仁之用寧有既乎？有所不爲，即無穿窬之心也。人能推所不爲，以達於所爲，而至于事事皆不爲焉，則能滿其無穿窬之心，而行無不宜矣。義之用寧有窮乎？是則仁義之心，人所固有。茍有之而不能推，推之而不能充，而以爲未嘗有仁義焉者，是豈人之本心哉？大抵人有是心，莫非全體。雖包括天地，兼利萬物，亦其能事也。然有所蔽，而不能盡乎此心之量，則恩及禽獸而功不至于百姓，耻受嘑蹴而義不辨乎萬鍾
translation_en:
…is the beginning of benevolence. Everyone possesses it, and so everyone has things they cannot bear to do. Yet, constrained by their material endowment and obscured by external things, people may shrink from doing one thing while tolerating another. If they simply extend this unwillingness to what they currently tolerate, their heart of compassion will encounter no obstruction or obscuration, and all will be benevolence. The heart that feels shame and dislikes wrongdoing is the beginning of righteousness. Everyone possesses it, and so everyone has things they refuse to do. Yet, with their understanding led astray and themselves transformed by external things, people may refuse to do one thing while doing another. If they simply extend this refusal to what they currently do, their heart of shame and dislike of wrongdoing will encounter no impediment, and all will be righteousness.

To have things one cannot bear to do is precisely to have a heart without any desire to harm others. If people can extend this unwillingness to what they currently tolerate, until they cannot bear to inflict harm in any matter, they can fully develop their heart that has no desire to harm others, and their love will embrace everyone. How could the application of benevolence ever be exhausted? To have things one refuses to do is precisely to have a heart without any inclination to break through walls or climb over them to steal. If people can extend this refusal to what they currently do, until they refuse wrongdoing in every matter, they can bring to fullness their heart that has no inclination to theft, and all their conduct will be fitting. How could the application of righteousness ever reach its limit?

Thus, the heart of benevolence and righteousness is something people inherently possess. If they possess it but cannot extend it, or extend it but cannot develop it fully, and then suppose that they have never possessed benevolence and righteousness, could this be their original heart? In general, everyone possesses this heart in its entirety. Even encompassing Heaven and Earth and benefiting all things alike lies within its powers. Yet if it is obscured and people cannot fully realize its capacity, then kindness may reach birds and beasts while its benefits fail to reach the common people; they may feel ashamed to accept food offered with a contemptuous shout or a kick, yet fail to distinguish what is righteous when offered a salary of ten thousand measures of grain…

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
者有矣是皆不善推其所爲也故孟子教人因
其善端之發而悉推之以各造乎其極則天之
所以與我者可以無不盡矣說者謂孟子平生
受用惟在善推所爲一語觀此尤信
易
敦復无悔中以自考也
張燮
同考試官訓導俞批自考就復上立說
非膚見可到
===
同考試官教諭魏批敦復自考原無二
道是作能知之而辭又醞藉宜錄出以破群疑
考試官教諭姜批詞不費而意盡
考試官教諭徐批深得象傳申爻之
旨
論復之厚而无慊於內惟中之成而无待於外
此易象之旨也盖復不外乎中德也今以中德
而自成於已豈非復之厚而无慊於內者乎且
夫復之六五中順居尊當復之時周公繫以敦
punctuated:
者有矣。是皆不善推其所爲也。故孟子教人因其善端之發，而悉推之，以各造乎其極，則天之所以與我者，可以無不盡矣。說者謂孟子平生受用，惟在「善推所爲」一語，觀此尤信。

易
敦復无悔，中以自考也。
張燮

同考試官訓導俞批：自考就復上立說，非膚見可到。
同考試官教諭魏批：敦復自考，原無二道。是作能知之，而辭又醞藉，宜錄出以破群疑。
考試官教諭姜批：詞不費而意盡。
考試官教諭徐批：深得《象傳》申爻之旨。

論復之厚而无慊於內，惟中之成而无待於外，此《易》象之旨也。盖復不外乎中德也。今以中德而自成於已，豈非復之厚而无慊於內者乎？且夫復之六五，中順居尊，當復之時，周公繫以敦
translation_en:
…there are such people. All this results from failing to extend properly what one already does. Thus Mencius taught people to take the emergence of their beginnings of goodness and extend them fully, bringing each to its utmost reach. Then everything Heaven has endowed us with can be fully realized. Commentators say that what Mencius relied upon throughout his life lay solely in the phrase “properly extending what one already does.” This passage makes that claim especially convincing.

Book of Changes
“Steadfast in returning, without regret”: through centrality one brings oneself to completion.
Zhang Xie 張燮

Comment by Associate Examiner Yu, Assistant Instructor: The discussion of bringing oneself to completion is grounded in returning. Such an understanding is beyond the reach of superficial insight.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wei, Instructor: Steadfast returning and bringing oneself to completion are fundamentally not two different ways. This composition understands that, and its language is also rich in implication. It should be included in the record to dispel the doubts of others.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Instructor: The language is economical, yet the meaning is fully expressed.

Comment by Examiner Xu, Instructor: It profoundly grasps the intent with which the Commentary on the Images elucidates the line statement.

To discuss depth in returning and the absence of dissatisfaction within: this rests solely on attaining completion through centrality, without depending on anything external. Such is the intent of the Image commentary in the Book of Changes. Returning, indeed, does not lie outside the virtue of centrality. Now, when one brings oneself to completion through this virtue, is this not depth in returning, with no dissatisfaction within? Moreover, the six in the fifth place of the hexagram Return is central and yielding and occupies the position of honor. In the time of returning, the Duke of Zhou attached to it the words “steadfast…”

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
復无悔之辭矣孔子象傳申之意謂二雖休復
未必其能敦也五則敦厚於復而善心渾乎其
恒存不困於心而衡於慮也尚何悔之内出乎
四雖獨復未必其能厚也五則篤厚於復而善
行慥乎其純篤不徵於色而發於聲也又何悔
之可憂乎其若是者豈有他哉亦惟中以自成
而已盖六五以柔順之爻得居中之道如不偏
不倚中之具於心者也向也内欲一萌有時而
或忘矣今則自成其中而復於既忘之後未嘗
===
暫得而暫失焉無過不及中之見於行者也向
也外物一交有時而或失矣今則自考其中而
復於既失之餘未嘗屢失而屢復焉善心自存
而中之體以立不假人以交脩也豈若二之下
仁而為休復者乎善行自篤而中之用以行不
資人以相輔也豈若四之從道而為獨復者乎
吁以得中之道而致自成之功此所以為敦復
之象无悔之道也傳象者舉爻辭而申之明矣
抑論之人受天地之中以生中本人之所固有
punctuated:
復无悔之辭矣。孔子象傳申之，意謂二雖休復，未必其能敦也；五則敦厚於復，而善心渾乎其恒存，不困於心而衡於慮也，尚何悔之内出乎？四雖獨復，未必其能厚也；五則篤厚於復，而善行慥乎其純篤，不徵於色而發於聲也，又何悔之可憂乎？其若是者，豈有他哉？亦惟中以自成而已。盖六五以柔順之爻，得居中之道，如不偏不倚，中之具於心者也。向也内欲一萌，有時而或忘矣；今則自成其中，而復於既忘之後，未嘗暫得而暫失焉。無過不及，中之見於行者也。向也外物一交，有時而或失矣；今則自考其中，而復於既失之餘，未嘗屢失而屢復焉。善心自存，而中之體以立，不假人以交脩也，豈若二之下仁而為休復者乎？善行自篤，而中之用以行，不資人以相輔也，豈若四之從道而為獨復者乎？吁！以得中之道，而致自成之功，此所以為敦復之象、无悔之道也。傳象者舉爻辭而申之，明矣。

抑論之，人受天地之中以生，中本人之所固有
translation_en:
…the words, “Return with earnestness; no regret.” Confucius elaborates upon them in the Commentary on the Images. His meaning is that although the second line represents an admirable return, it does not necessarily achieve earnestness. The fifth, however, is earnest and steadfast in returning: its good intentions remain constantly present in their wholeness, without distress of heart or vexation of thought. What regret could still arise within? Although the fourth line represents returning alone, it does not necessarily achieve steadfastness. The fifth, however, is firm and steadfast in returning: its good conduct is sincere and resolute in its purity and earnestness, without distress showing in the countenance or finding expression in the voice. What regret, then, could give cause for concern? Is there any other reason for its being thus? It is simply that it perfects itself through centrality.

The yielding and compliant line, six in the fifth place, attains the Way of occupying the center. Being neither partial nor inclined to either side exemplifies centrality as it is embodied in the heart. Formerly, whenever an inward desire arose, this centrality might sometimes be forgotten. Now, however, the line itself perfects its centrality and returns to it after it has been forgotten, never gaining it briefly only to lose it again. Having neither excess nor deficiency exemplifies centrality as it appears in conduct. Formerly, whenever contact with external things occurred, this centrality might sometimes be lost. Now, however, the line examines its own centrality [?] and returns to it after its loss, never repeatedly losing it and repeatedly returning to it. Good intentions persist of themselves, and thereby the substance of centrality is established, without relying on others for mutual cultivation. How could this be like the second line, which achieves an admirable return by placing itself below one who is benevolent? Good conduct becomes steadfast of itself, and thereby the functioning of centrality is put into practice, without depending on others for assistance. How could this be like the fourth line, which returns alone by following the Way?

Ah! By attaining the Way of centrality, it accomplishes the work of perfecting itself. This is what constitutes the image of earnest return and the Way of having no regret. The author of the Commentary on the Images cites the line statement and elaborates upon it: the meaning is clear.

To discuss this further: human beings receive the centrality of Heaven and Earth at birth; centrality is fundamentally inherent in human beings…

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
也但有生之後氣稟拘之物欲蔽之聖賢而下
能復本然之中者幾何人哉六五之中雖或失
之而能復之不徒復之而能敦之其天資之美
不可誣也求之古人其成湯之改過不吝武王
之以義勝欲者歟
兼三才而兩之故易六畫而成卦分陰分
陽迭用柔剛故易六位而成章
王忠
同考試官訓導俞批人知六畫有三才
===
而不知六位亦有二才也此篇認理分明措辭
醇雅其深於易者歟
同考試官教諭魏批倍六畫分六位正
聖人作易順性命處場中罕有得此意者發明
精切無踰此篇
考試官教諭姜批體認明白
考試官教諭徐批理到之言自別
聖人作易以順理有見於卦畫之重者有見於
爻位之分者盖聖人作易重之則為六畫分之
punctuated:
也。但有生之後，氣稟拘之，物欲蔽之，聖賢而下，能復本然之中者幾何人哉？六五之中，雖或失之，而能復之；不徒復之，而能敦之，其天資之美不可誣也。求之古人，其成湯之改過不吝、武王之以義勝欲者歟？

兼三才而兩之，故易六畫而成卦；分陰分陽，迭用柔剛，故易六位而成章。
王忠

同考試官訓導俞批：人知六畫有三才，而不知六位亦有二才也。此篇認理分明，措辭醇雅，其深於易者歟？

同考試官教諭魏批：倍六畫，分六位，正聖人作易順性命處。場中罕有得此意者，發明精切，無踰此篇。

考試官教諭姜批：體認明白。

考試官教諭徐批：理到之言自別。

聖人作易以順理，有見於卦畫之重者，有見於爻位之分者。盖聖人作易，重之則為六畫，分之
translation_en:
…Yet after birth, people are constrained by their endowment of vital energy and obscured by material desires. Below the sages and worthies, how many can recover their original equilibrium? Although the equilibrium of the yielding fifth line may sometimes be lost, it can be recovered; not merely recovered, but made firm. The excellence of its innate endowment cannot be denied. If we seek examples among the ancients, would they not be Cheng Tang, who corrected his faults without hesitation, and King Wu, who overcame desire through righteousness?

“The Three Powers are combined and each doubled; thus, in the Changes, six lines form a hexagram. Yin and yang are distinguished, and the yielding and the firm are employed alternately; thus, in the Changes, the six positions form a patterned whole.”
By Wang Zhong.

Comment by Associate Examiner Yu, Assistant Instructor: People know that the six lines contain the Three Powers, but do not know that the six positions also contain the Two Powers [?]. This essay apprehends the principles distinctly, and its diction is pure and elegant. Surely its author has a profound understanding of the Changes!

Comment by Associate Examiner Wei, Instructor: Doubling to produce six lines and differentiating six positions are precisely where the sages, in composing the Changes, followed the principles of human nature and destiny. Few in the examination hall have grasped this meaning. For precise and penetrating elucidation, no essay surpasses this one.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Instructor: The understanding is clear.

Comment by Examiner Xu, Instructor: Words that fully grasp the principles are distinctive in themselves.

When the sages composed the Changes to accord with principle, they perceived something in the doubling of the lines of the trigrams, and something in the differentiation of the line positions. For when the sages composed the Changes, doubling them produced six lines; differentiating them…

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
則爲六位也然則卦爻之間何莫而非性命之
理哉昔吾夫子說卦論聖人作易以順性命之
理及此謂夫聖人之作易也既成三畫之卦巳
具三才之象由是因而重之兼三才而爲兩三
才引而伸之倍三畫而爲兩三畫以上二爻爲
天天道以兩而成象也以中二爻爲人人道以
兩而成德也以下二爻爲地地道以兩而成質
也是以一内一外而大成之卦以備有貞有悔
而全體之象以立豈非六畫而成卦乎然此特
===
統言之耳又細分之陰位半於陽陽位半於陰
而陰陽之中分剛位間於柔柔位間於剛而剛
柔之迭用五陽上陰天道相間而立於上矣三
仁四義人道相間而立於中矣初剛二柔地道
相間而立於下矣是以陰陽經緯燦然而可觀
剛柔間雜蔚然而可覩豈非六位而成章乎是
則卦之重者此三才也爻之分者此三才也聖
人作易以順性命之理豈不從可見哉大抵易
書不外乎卦爻而卦爻不外乎三才三才也者
punctuated: 則爲六位也。然則卦爻之間，何莫而非性命之理哉？昔吾夫子說卦，論聖人作易以順性命之理，及此，謂夫聖人之作易也，既成三畫之卦，巳具三才之象。由是因而重之，兼三才而爲兩三才；引而伸之，倍三畫而爲兩三畫。以上二爻爲天，天道以兩而成象也；以中二爻爲人，人道以兩而成德也；以下二爻爲地，地道以兩而成質也。是以一内一外，而大成之卦以備；有貞有悔，而全體之象以立。豈非六畫而成卦乎？然此特統言之耳。又細分之，陰位半於陽，陽位半於陰，而陰陽之中分；剛位間於柔，柔位間於剛，而剛柔之迭用。五陽上陰，天道相間而立於上矣；三仁四義，人道相間而立於中矣；初剛二柔，地道相間而立於下矣。是以陰陽經緯，燦然而可觀；剛柔間雜，蔚然而可覩。豈非六位而成章乎？是則卦之重者，此三才也；爻之分者，此三才也。聖人作易以順性命之理，豈不從可見哉？大抵易書不外乎卦爻，而卦爻不外乎三才。三才也者，
translation_en:
…then there are six positions. Thus, among the hexagrams and their lines, what is not an expression of the principles of human nature and destiny? Formerly, in Explaining the Trigrams, our Master discussed how the sages made the Book of Changes to accord with the principles of human nature and destiny. On reaching this point, he meant that, when the sages made the Changes, once they had formed the three-line trigrams, these already embodied images of the Three Powers: Heaven, humanity, and Earth. Proceeding from this, they doubled them, taking the Three Powers together and making two sets of Three Powers; extending them further, they doubled the three lines to make two sets of three lines. They assigned the upper two lines to Heaven: the Way of Heaven forms its images through a pair. They assigned the middle two lines to humanity: the Way of humanity achieves its virtue through a pair. They assigned the lower two lines to Earth: the Way of Earth forms its substance through a pair. Thus, with one inner and one outer trigram, the fully developed hexagram was complete; with the lower trigram, zhen, and the upper trigram, hui, the image of the whole was established. Is this not how six lines form a hexagram? Yet this is only a general account.

Distinguishing them more finely, yin positions occupy one half and yang positions the other, so that yin and yang are equally divided. Firm positions alternate with yielding ones, and yielding positions with firm ones, so that firmness and yielding operate in alternation. The fifth position is yang and the top position yin: the Way of Heaven is established above through their alternation. The third is benevolence and the fourth righteousness: the Way of humanity is established in the middle through their alternation. The first is firm and the second yielding: the Way of Earth is established below through their alternation. Thus yin and yang form a warp and weft, brilliantly visible; firmness and yielding intermingle in a richly apparent pattern. Is this not how six positions form an ordered pattern? Thus, what is doubled in the hexagrams is these Three Powers; what is distinguished in the line positions is these Three Powers. Can we not see from this how the sages made the Changes to accord with the principles of human nature and destiny? In general, the Book of Changes does not go beyond hexagrams and lines, and hexagrams and lines do not go beyond the Three Powers. As for the Three Powers…

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
形而上之理也卦爻也者形而下之器也理非
器不形器非理不立故聖人作易以有形之卦
爻而順无形之性命此易所以爲性命之源也
世之論者以卜筮而小吾易烏足與言易哉
書
在璿璣玉衡以齊七政
戴大賓
同考試官教諭李批七政自有常度察
璣衡以齊之恐曆法有差爾此作能知此意便
===
有此詞是宜錄之
同考試官學正王批觀象爲授時計作
者不知以七政為在器之象殊戾本旨惟此篇
卓有定見且詞氣渾融誠璧經中之巨擘歟
考試官教諭姜批詞氣寛平必佳士也
考試官教諭徐批不戾經傳佳作
察象之在器者以合象之在天者此聖人之初
政也甚矣天象之難定也使不察器以合之其
何以爲曆象授時之計哉史臣記聖人之初政
punctuated:
形而上之理也；卦爻也者，形而下之器也。理非器不形，器非理不立。故聖人作易，以有形之卦爻而順无形之性命，此易所以爲性命之源也。世之論者以卜筮而小吾易，烏足與言易哉！

書
在璿璣玉衡，以齊七政。
戴大賓

同考試官教諭李批：七政自有常度，察璣衡以齊之，恐曆法有差爾。此作能知此意，便有此詞，是宜錄之。

同考試官學正王批：觀象爲授時計。作者不知，以七政為在器之象，殊戾本旨。惟此篇卓有定見，且詞氣渾融，誠璧經中之巨擘歟！

考試官教諭姜批：詞氣寛平，必佳士也。

考試官教諭徐批：不戾經傳，佳作。

察象之在器者，以合象之在天者，此聖人之初政也。甚矣，天象之難定也！使不察器以合之，其何以爲曆象授時之計哉？史臣記聖人之初政
translation_en:
…are principles above physical form; the hexagrams and their lines are concrete instruments below physical form. Without instruments, principles cannot become manifest; without principles, instruments cannot stand. Thus, in making the Changes, the sage used the visible hexagrams and lines to accord with the formless nature and destiny. This is why the Changes is the source of nature and destiny. Those commentators who belittle our Changes as mere divination—how could they be worthy of discussing it?

Documents
“He examined the jade-adorned rotating instrument and jade sighting tube, to bring the seven celestial regulators into accord.”
Dai Dabin

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Instructor: The seven celestial regulators inherently have their constant measures. Examining the rotating instrument and sighting tube to bring them into accord is simply a precaution against errors in calendrical methods. This composition understands that meaning and consequently expresses it in these words. It deserves to be included.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, School Director: Observing celestial configurations serves the purpose of granting the seasons to the people. Writers who fail to understand this take the seven celestial regulators to be the representations on the instrument, greatly contradicting the original purport. This essay alone shows an outstandingly firm grasp; moreover, its language and spirit form a seamless whole. Surely it ranks among the foremost compositions on this classic [?; transcribed as 璧經]!

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Instructor: The language and spirit are expansive and even-tempered. He must be a fine scholar.

Comment by Examiner Xu, Instructor: It does not contradict the classic or its commentaries. A fine composition.

To examine the configurations represented on the instrument and bring them into agreement with the configurations in heaven: this was the sage’s first act of government. How very difficult it is to establish celestial configurations precisely! If one did not examine the instrument to bring them into agreement, how could one devise a means of calculating celestial movements, observing their configurations, and granting the seasons to the people? The court historian recorded the sage’s first act of government…

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
如此盖謂爲治莫先於治曆治曆莫要於觀象
彼璣之爲器以璿飾之其制則東西運轉所以
象天而載七政也衡之爲管以玉爲之其制則
南北低昂所以窺璣而齊七政也然歲久易湮
不能無差舜則精以察之竭心思於推步之時
而象之或遲或速皆有以知其度數之詳世遠
易弛不能無異舜則明以審之竭目力於窺測
之際而象之或順或逆皆有以知其次舍之位
所以然者盖日月運行於天有遲有速今焉察
===
之器以驗諸天其度數果合歟否歟必使上下
之間遲速爲之一致也五星運行於天有順有
逆今焉審之璣以徵諸天其次舍果同歟異歟
必使上下之際順逆爲之不爽也高遠難知者
即諸器而可知法制易見者驗諸天而益合夫
然則天時以定曆法以審人時不於此而授哉
舜之急先務有如此夫大抵天下之政未有重
於人時者苟曆法不定則時有不正四時一失
萬事俱爽尚何以撫五辰而成天下之治哉故
punctuated: 如此。盖謂爲治莫先於治曆，治曆莫要於觀象。彼璣之爲器，以璿飾之，其制則東西運轉，所以象天而載七政也。衡之爲管，以玉爲之，其制則南北低昂，所以窺璣而齊七政也。然歲久易湮，不能無差，舜則精以察之，竭心思於推步之時，而象之或遲或速，皆有以知其度數之詳。世遠易弛，不能無異，舜則明以審之，竭目力於窺測之際，而象之或順或逆，皆有以知其次舍之位。所以然者，盖日月運行於天，有遲有速，今焉察之器以驗諸天，其度數果合歟否歟？必使上下之間，遲速爲之一致也。五星運行於天，有順有逆，今焉審之璣以徵諸天，其次舍果同歟異歟？必使上下之際，順逆爲之不爽也。高遠難知者，即諸器而可知；法制易見者，驗諸天而益合。夫然則天時以定，曆法以審，人時不於此而授哉？舜之急先務有如此夫！大抵天下之政，未有重於人時者。苟曆法不定，則時有不正，四時一失，萬事俱爽，尚何以撫五辰而成天下之治哉？故
translation_en:
…in this way. The meaning is that, in governing, nothing takes precedence over regulating the calendar, and in regulating the calendar, nothing is more essential than observing celestial configurations. The revolving instrument, the ji, is adorned with fine jade. Its construction allows it to turn east and west, thereby representing the heavens and carrying representations of the seven celestial regulators—the sun, moon, and five planets. The sighting tube, the heng, is made of jade. Its construction allows it to be lowered and raised toward north and south, thereby enabling observations through the ji and bringing the seven celestial regulators into alignment.

Yet over many years, knowledge readily becomes obscured, and discrepancies are inevitable. Shun therefore examined the instrument meticulously, devoting all his mental powers to astronomical calculations, so that he could know in detail the measured degrees of celestial movements, whether slow or fast. Across distant generations, practices readily become lax, and divergences are inevitable. Shun therefore scrutinized it discerningly, exerting his eyesight fully in observation and measurement, so that he could know the positions of the celestial bodies in their stations and lodges, whether their movements were direct or retrograde.

The reason is that the sun and moon move through the heavens at varying speeds. By now examining them on the instrument and checking against the heavens, he asked whether their measured degrees actually agreed or not. He invariably ensured that the speeds above and below corresponded. The five planets move through the heavens with both direct and retrograde motion. By now scrutinizing them on the ji and verifying against the heavens, he asked whether their stations and lodges actually coincided or differed. He invariably ensured that direct and retrograde motions above and below matched without discrepancy. What was lofty, distant, and difficult to know could be known by consulting the instrument; the readily visible arrangements of the instrument could be checked against the heavens and brought into still closer agreement. Thus the celestial seasons were determined and calendrical methods verified. Was this not how the proper times for human activities were made known? Such was Shun’s urgency in attending to what must come first!

In general, among all the affairs of government under Heaven, none is weightier than the proper timing of human activities. If calendrical methods are not settled, the reckoning of time will be incorrect. Once the four seasons are misreckoned, every undertaking goes awry. How then could one order the five celestial periods and bring about good government throughout the realm? Therefore…

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
堯即位而曆象授時舜攝位而察器齊政皆此
意也噫庶績咸熙無為而治良有以哉有天下
者其致意焉
六卿分職各率其屬以倡九牧阜成兆民
六年五服一朝又六年王乃時巡考制度
于四岳諸侯各朝于方岳大明黜陟
黃肯堂
同考試官教諭李批此題作者類多以
體統保治立說殊戾本旨是篇認理明白而文
===
足以發之蓋究心于經學者允宜錄出
同考試官學正王批此篇約繁就簡寫
出成王訓迪百官之意前後相貫文采爛然錄
之以範來學
考試官教諭姜批周官內外相維意
政如此
考試官教諭徐批發明訓迪建官體
統處甚是
賢王訓迪建官之體統在內者有其要在外者
punctuated:
堯即位而曆象授時，舜攝位而察器齊政，皆此意也。噫！庶績咸熙，無為而治，良有以哉！有天下者，其致意焉。

六卿分職，各率其屬，以倡九牧，阜成兆民。六年，五服一朝；又六年，王乃時巡，考制度于四岳。諸侯各朝于方岳，大明黜陟。

黃肯堂

同考試官教諭李批：此題作者類多以體統保治立說，殊戾本旨。是篇認理明白，而文足以發之，蓋究心于經學者，允宜錄出。

同考試官學正王批：此篇約繁就簡，寫出成王訓迪百官之意，前後相貫，文采爛然，錄之以範來學。

考試官教諭姜批：周官內外相維，意政如此。

考試官教諭徐批：發明訓迪建官體統處甚是。

賢王訓迪建官之體統，在內者有其要，在外者
translation_en:
…When Yao ascended the throne, he calculated and observed the celestial movements and announced the seasons; when Shun assumed the regency, he examined the instruments and brought the celestial regulators into accord. Both acted with this intention. Ah! There was good reason why all undertakings flourished and order prevailed without deliberate intervention! Those who possess All under Heaven should give this their attention.

The six ministers divide their duties, each leading his subordinates to set an example for the nine regional governors and to enrich and perfect the lives of the myriad people. Every six years, those of the five service zones attend court once. After another six years, the king makes a timely tour of inspection, examining institutions and standards at the Four Sacred Peaks. The regional lords each attend him at the sacred peak of their quarter, and demotions and promotions are made unmistakably clear.

Huang Kentang

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Instructor: Those writing on this topic mostly frame their arguments around hierarchical organization and the preservation of good government, seriously departing from its original intent. This essay understands the principles clearly, and its prose adequately brings them out. Its author has evidently devoted himself to the study of the Classics; it certainly deserves to be selected for inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor: This essay reduces complexity to simplicity, conveying King Cheng’s intention in instructing and guiding the hundred officials. Its beginning and end are coherently connected, and its literary brilliance shines forth. It is included to serve as a model for future students.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Instructor: The offices of Zhou supported one another at court and in the provinces; the intended governance was like this [?].

Comment by Examiner Xu, Instructor: The exposition of instruction and guidance concerning the hierarchical organization of established offices is particularly sound.

The worthy king instructed and guided his officials concerning the hierarchical organization of established offices. For those at court there were essential principles; for those outside the court…

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
有其法盖率屬圖治之要朝巡考課之法六卿
諸侯所當知者也成王各訓迪之有以哉昔成
王訓官之意謂夫致治莫要於建官建官莫先
於體統但内外不同體統亦異自六卿言之内
則統領乎群工外則管攝乎州牧彼曰治曰教
曰禮既各分其職矣必率其屬以為九牧之倡
使皆率屬以趨事焉曰政曰禁曰土既各分其
任矣必統其屬以為九牧之先使皆統屬以赴
工焉自内達外政治脩明而兆民之衆莫不歸
===
於阜厚也由近及遠教化浹洽而黎庶之繁莫
不底於化成也如此則六卿之體統立矣自諸
侯言之定以六年五服一朝會于京師又歴六
年王者乃時巡于四岳凡治也教也禮也悉有
以考其廢興而諸侯各朝于方岳之下凡禁也
政也土也咸有以稽其脩否而諸侯各覲于方
岳之前其有不職者則罰以懲之而大明其黜
之之法其有脩職者則賞以勸之而大明其陟
之之典如此則諸侯之體統立矣吁六卿治内
punctuated: 有其法。盖率屬圖治之要、朝巡考課之法，六卿諸侯所當知者也。成王各訓迪之，有以哉！昔成王訓官之意，謂夫致治莫要於建官，建官莫先於體統。但内外不同，體統亦異。自六卿言之，内則統領乎群工，外則管攝乎州牧。彼曰治、曰教、曰禮，既各分其職矣，必率其屬，以為九牧之倡，使皆率屬以趨事焉。曰政、曰禁、曰土，既各分其任矣，必統其屬，以為九牧之先，使皆統屬以赴工焉。自内達外，政治脩明，而兆民之衆莫不歸於阜厚也；由近及遠，教化浹洽，而黎庶之繁莫不底於化成也。如此，則六卿之體統立矣。自諸侯言之，定以六年，五服一朝，會于京師；又歴六年，王者乃時巡于四岳。凡治也、教也、禮也，悉有以考其廢興，而諸侯各朝于方岳之下；凡禁也、政也、土也，咸有以稽其脩否，而諸侯各覲于方岳之前。其有不職者，則罰以懲之，而大明其黜之之法；其有脩職者，則賞以勸之，而大明其陟之之典。如此，則諸侯之體統立矣。吁！六卿治内，
translation_en:
…have their prescribed rules. For the essentials of leading subordinates in pursuit of good government, and the rules for court audiences, royal inspection tours, and assessments of performance, are matters that the six ministers and the feudal lords ought to understand. King Cheng had good reason to instruct and guide each of them!

The intention behind King Cheng’s instruction of officials was this: nothing is more essential to achieving good government than establishing offices, and in establishing offices nothing takes precedence over the ordering of authority. Yet the court and the outer domains differ, and so too do their respective hierarchies. As for the six ministers, within the court they command the assembled officials; beyond it they oversee the regional governors. Those responsible for administration, instruction, and ritual each have their separate duties, but must lead their subordinates and set an example for the governors of the nine regions, so that all will lead their own subordinates diligently in attending to affairs. Those responsible for military affairs, prohibitions, and lands each have their separate responsibilities, but must command their subordinates and take the lead for the nine regional governors, so that all will command their own subordinates in carrying out their work. From the court to the outer domains, government will be well ordered and enlightened, and the multitude of the people will all attain prosperity. From near to far, moral instruction will permeate everywhere, and the entire populace will attain moral transformation. In this way, the hierarchy of the six ministers will be established.

As for the feudal lords, it is prescribed that every six years those of the five zones of service shall attend court once, assembling in the capital. After another six years, the king shall make inspection tours in the appropriate seasons to the four sacred peaks. Administration, instruction, and ritual will all be examined to determine whether they have fallen into neglect or flourished, and the feudal lords will each attend court at the foot of their region’s sacred peak. Prohibitions, military affairs, and lands will all be scrutinized to determine whether they have been properly attended to, and the feudal lords will each appear in audience before their region’s sacred peak. Those who fail in their duties will receive punishment to admonish them, clearly manifesting the rules for their demotion; those who fulfill their duties will receive rewards to encourage them, clearly manifesting the regulations for their promotion. In this way, the hierarchy of the feudal lords will be established.

Ah! The six ministers govern within…

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
諸侯治外内外相承體統不紊制治保邦之道
孰有要于此哉成王其善于訓官者矣嗟夫爲
政固當任人又當任法唐虞之時二十二人之
咨任人也三載九載之制任法也故當時庶績
咸煕萬國咸寧固由于建官之得人實由于人
法之並任成王訓迪建官體統而有及于考課
之法亦此意也世稱泰和之治者必曰虞周其
以是歟
詩
===
豈敢定居一月三捷
陳良山
同考試官教諭杜批筆力老健說理詳
明周王以義遣戍之意宛然在目佳作也
同考試官教諭羅批周王遣戍何等精
神氣燄此作模寫得出豈胷中有幾萬甲兵者
耶
考試官教諭姜批得周人風諭戍卒
之意讀之令人勃勃生氣得士如此吾豈憂戎
punctuated:
諸侯治外，内外相承，體統不紊，制治保邦之道，孰有要于此哉？成王其善于訓官者矣！嗟夫！爲政固當任人，又當任法。唐虞之時，二十二人之咨，任人也；三載九載之制，任法也。故當時庶績咸煕，萬國咸寧，固由于建官之得人，實由于人法之並任。成王訓迪建官體統，而有及于考課之法，亦此意也。世稱泰和之治者，必曰虞周，其以是歟？

詩

豈敢定居？一月三捷。
陳良山

同考試官教諭杜批：筆力老健，說理詳明，周王以義遣戍之意，宛然在目，佳作也。

同考試官教諭羅批：周王遣戍，何等精神氣燄！此作模寫得出，豈胷中有幾萬甲兵者耶？

考試官教諭姜批：得周人風諭戍卒之意，讀之令人勃勃生氣。得士如此，吾豈憂戎
translation_en:
…the regional lords govern beyond the royal domain. With those within and without supporting one another and the hierarchy remaining orderly, what could be more essential to establishing good government and preserving the realm? King Cheng was indeed skilled at instructing his officials! Ah! In governing, one must certainly rely on people, but one must also rely on regulations. In the time of Tang Yao and Yu Shun, consulting the twenty-two men exemplified reliance on people; the system of three-year and nine-year evaluations exemplified reliance on regulations. Thus, all undertakings flourished and the myriad states enjoyed peace. This certainly resulted from finding suitable men to fill offices, but it truly depended on employing both people and regulations. King Cheng’s instructions on the hierarchy of established offices also extended to methods of evaluating official performance: they expressed this same intention. Whenever later generations speak of government that achieved great harmony, they invariably cite Yu and Zhou. Is this not the reason?

The Book of Odes

“How dare we settle down at ease? In one month, three victories.”
By Chen Liangshan

Comment by Associate Examiner Du, Instructor: His writing is mature and vigorous, and his exposition of principle is detailed and clear. The Zhou king’s intention in dispatching troops for garrison service in accordance with righteousness appears vividly before our eyes. An excellent composition.

Comment by Associate Examiner Luo, Instructor: What spirit and martial ardor the Zhou king displayed in dispatching the garrison troops! This composition succeeds in capturing them. Could its author be a man who holds tens of thousands of armored soldiers in his breast?

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Instructor: This captures the intention of the men of Zhou in exhorting the garrison soldiers through verse. Reading it fills one with surging vigor. With men such as these, why should I worry about hostile forces…

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
九重無北顧之憂也兵威遠振于邊庭而戎馬
無南牧之患也夫如是則多難以紓成事以定
中國豈有不尊疆圉豈有不靖者哉周王歌此
於遣戍之日其真得鼓舞激勸之道也歟大抵
兵事以哀敬為本而所尚則威此章之一月三
捷作其奮揚之威也下章之豈不日戒動其戒
懼之心也敬勇相資並行不悖此行師之要御
戎之道也嚴尤顧謂周得中策然則如何而為
策之上書曰明王慎德四夷咸賓策之上者其
===
在茲耶
卬盛于豆于豆于登其香始升上帝居歆
黃鞏
同考試官教諭杜批周人奉祭格天之
意類能言之而詞氣舂容親切有味者僅見此
篇
同考試官教諭羅批能以配饗疊講
且詞氣溫純典則要非初學可到
考試官教諭姜批詞氣溫柔敦厚蓋
punctuated:
九重無北顧之憂也，兵威遠振于邊庭，而戎馬無南牧之患也。夫如是，則多難以紓，成事以定，中國豈有不尊、疆圉豈有不靖者哉？周王歌此於遣戍之日，其真得鼓舞激勸之道也歟！大抵兵事以哀敬為本，而所尚則威。此章之「一月三捷」，作其奮揚之威也；下章之「豈不日戒」，動其戒懼之心也。敬勇相資，並行不悖，此行師之要、御戎之道也。嚴尤顧謂周得中策，然則如何而為策之上？《書》曰：「明王慎德，四夷咸賓。」策之上者，其在茲耶？
卬盛于豆，于豆于登，其香始升，上帝居歆。
黃鞏
同考試官教諭杜批：周人奉祭格天之意，類能言之，而詞氣舂容、親切有味者，僅見此篇。
同考試官教諭羅批：能以配饗疊講，且詞氣溫純典則，要非初學可到。
考試官教諭姜批：詞氣溫柔敦厚，蓋
translation_en:
…The imperial palace will have no anxiety over the north; military might will resound far across the frontier, and there will be no danger of enemy cavalry pasturing southward. If this is so, the many troubles will be relieved and accomplished affairs secured. How could the Central States fail to command respect, or the frontiers fail to be pacified? When the king of Zhou sang this on the day he dispatched the garrison troops, surely he truly understood how to inspire and encourage them! In general, military affairs are founded upon compassion and reverence, while what they prize is awe-inspiring might. This stanza’s “three victories in one month” arouses their spirited might; the following stanza’s “How could we fail to be vigilant each day?” stirs their vigilance and apprehension. Reverence and courage sustain each other and operate together without conflict: this is the essential principle of conducting campaigns and the way to ward off the Rong. Yet Yan You called Zhou’s approach a middling strategy. What, then, would constitute the highest strategy? The Book of Documents says: “When an enlightened king attends carefully to his virtue, the barbarians of all four quarters come in submission.” Does the highest strategy perhaps lie here?
“We fill the dou vessels, the dou vessels and the deng vessels; their fragrance begins to rise, and the Lord on High accepts them with pleasure.”
Huang Gong
Comment by Associate Examiner Du, Instructor: Most can articulate the Zhou people’s intent in presenting sacrifices and reaching Heaven, but this is the only essay I have seen whose language and tone are spacious and unhurried, intimate and rich in meaning.
Comment by Associate Examiner Luo, Instructor: He is able to develop the exposition in successive layers through the theme of an ancestor sharing in the sacrificial offerings. Moreover, his language and tone are gentle, pure, and classically disciplined—an achievement certainly beyond a beginner.
Comment by Examiner Jiang, Instructor: The language and tone are gentle and kind, sincere and generous, for…

…the imperial palace is free from anxiety over the north; military might resounds far across the frontier, and there is no danger of enemy cavalry coming south to pasture their horses. If this is so, the many troubles can be relieved and garrison affairs settled. How could the central realm fail to be honored, or its borders fail to be secure? “I fill the dou vessels, the dou vessels and the deng vessels. As their fragrance begins to rise, the Lord on High accepts the offering.”
Huang Gong
Comment by Associate Examiner Du, Instructor: Most can express the idea that the people of Zhou reached Heaven through their sacrificial offerings. But only in this essay have I found language and a tone that are unhurried, intimate, and full of flavor.
Comment by Associate Examiner Luo, Instructor: He successfully brings the meaning of an ancestor’s sharing in the sacrificial offerings into his exposition. Moreover, his language and tone are gentle, pure, and in keeping with classical standards—certainly beyond the reach of a beginner.
Comment by Examiner Jiang, Instructor: The language and tone are gentle, warm, sincere, and generous, presumably …

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
有得於詩者也
考試官教諭徐批典則
祀禮方行而天心遂格周人尊祖配天之然也盖
奉祭莫難於格天也周人郊祀方行而格天之
速如此其亦有由然哉昔周公制禮尊后稷以
配天此則言其奉祭之事也謂夫我祖后稷克
配彼天今而尊事于南郊實能感孚乎上帝是
故祭必有豆所以薦菹醢也我則以菹醢而盛
之于豆祭必有登所以薦太羹也我則以太羹
===
而盛之于登或肆焉或將焉菹醢之芳臭始升
而圭璧未之或薦也以享焉以祀焉太羹之馨
香始達而歌樂未之或奏也斯時也感之遂通
而皇矣上帝居然其來歆假之即應而倬彼昊
天安然其來饗鑒精禋於沖漠之表盖與后稷
而相為陟降也曾謂高高在上而不吾應乎歆
祀事於對越之頃盖與后稷而相為上下也曾
謂蕩蕩難忱而莫予格乎夫莫大於郊也而薦
之之禮甚簡莫尊於帝也而饗之之應甚速是
punctuated:
有得於詩者也。
考試官教諭徐批：典則。
祀禮方行，而天心遂格，周人尊祖配天之然也。盖奉祭莫難於格天也。周人郊祀方行，而格天之速如此，其亦有由然哉！昔周公制禮，尊后稷以配天，此則言其奉祭之事也。謂夫我祖后稷，克配彼天，今而尊事于南郊，實能感孚乎上帝。是故祭必有豆，所以薦菹醢也；我則以菹醢而盛之于豆。祭必有登，所以薦太羹也；我則以太羹而盛之于登。或肆焉，或將焉，菹醢之芳臭始升，而圭璧未之或薦也；以享焉，以祀焉，太羹之馨香始達，而歌樂未之或奏也。斯時也，感之遂通，而皇矣上帝，居然其來歆；假之即應，而倬彼昊天，安然其來饗。鑒精禋於沖漠之表，盖與后稷而相為陟降也，曾謂高高在上而不吾應乎？歆祀事於對越之頃，盖與后稷而相為上下也，曾謂蕩蕩難忱而莫予格乎？夫莫大於郊也，而薦之之禮甚簡；莫尊於帝也，而饗之之應甚速。是
translation_en:
…is one who has gained an understanding of the Poetry.
Examiner Xu, Instructor, comments: “Exemplary and in accordance with the canons.”
The sacrificial rites had only just begun, yet Heaven’s heart was already moved to respond: such was the result [?] of the Zhou people’s honoring their ancestor by associating him with Heaven in sacrifice. In offering sacrifice, nothing is harder than moving Heaven to respond. Yet the Zhou people had scarcely begun their suburban sacrifice when Heaven responded so swiftly. Surely there was a reason for this! In former times, the Duke of Zhou established the rites and honored Hou Ji by associating him with Heaven in sacrifice. This passage speaks of their conduct of that sacrifice. It means that our ancestor Hou Ji was worthy of association with Heaven; now, reverently serving him at the southern suburban altar, we could truly move the Lord on High through our sincerity. Thus, sacrifice necessarily requires dou vessels, in which to offer pickled vegetables and meat sauces; we fill the dou vessels with these vegetables and sauces. Sacrifice necessarily requires deng vessels, in which to offer the Great Broth; we fill the deng vessels with that broth. As the offerings are set out and presented, the fragrance of the vegetables and sauces has only just begun to rise, and the jade tablets and disks have not yet been offered. As the offerings and sacrifices are made, the aroma of the Great Broth has only just begun to reach above, and the songs and music have not yet been performed. At this moment, the appeal immediately reaches its object, and the august Lord on High comes indeed to savor the offerings; the invocation brings an immediate response, and that lofty, vast Heaven comes serenely to partake. Beyond the bounds of the still and formless, he beholds the pure sacrifice, ascending and descending together with Hou Ji. Could one claim that he remains high above and does not respond to us? At the moment we reverently face him, he savors the sacrificial service, moving above and below together with Hou Ji. Could one claim that he is so vast as to be hard to trust and will not come to us? No sacrifice is greater than the suburban sacrifice, yet the rites for presenting its offerings are very simple. None is more exalted than the Lord on High, yet his response in accepting the offerings is very swift. This…

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
盖后稷之克饗天心之有素焉耳豈但芳臭之
薦信得其時哉雖然南郊祭天既配之以后稷
矣而明堂享帝則又配之以文王焉盖封國之
受始於后稷而王業之成由於文王以稷配天
所以尊稷也倣乎古也以文王配帝所以親文
王也以義起也尊尊親親兩盡其道此禮文之
所以備也此天心之所以格也此有周所以為
有道之長也
春秋
===
州公如曹〔桓公五年〕公會宰周公齊侯宋子
衛侯鄭伯許男曹伯于葵丘〔僖公九年〕
張天顯
同考試官教諭周批題有明傳作者率
欠融會冗碎厭觀此作能悉傳意而文理自然
接續屬比之教得之深矣
考試官教諭姜批理明詞健
考試官教諭徐批謹嚴
諸侯假朝禮春秋原所稱而録其本宰臣與會
punctuated:
盖后稷之克饗天心之有素焉耳，豈但芳臭之薦信得其時哉？雖然，南郊祭天，既配之以后稷矣，而明堂享帝，則又配之以文王焉。盖封國之受始於后稷，而王業之成由於文王。以稷配天，所以尊稷也，倣乎古也；以文王配帝，所以親文王也，以義起也。尊尊親親，兩盡其道，此禮文之所以備也，此天心之所以格也，此有周所以為有道之長也。

《春秋》

州公如曹〔桓公五年〕。公會宰周公、齊侯、宋子、衛侯、鄭伯、許男、曹伯于葵丘〔僖公九年〕。

張天顯

同考試官教諭周批：題有明傳，作者率欠融會，冗碎厭觀。此作能悉傳意，而文理自然接續，屬比之教得之深矣。

考試官教諭姜批：理明詞健。

考試官教諭徐批：謹嚴。

諸侯假朝禮，《春秋》原所稱而録其本；宰臣與會
translation_en:
…This was simply because Hou Ji had long been able to win acceptance from the heart of Heaven. How could it have been merely that the fragrant offerings were indeed presented at the proper time? Nevertheless, when Heaven was sacrificed to at the southern suburban altar, Hou Ji was associated with it in worship; when the Supreme Lord was offered worship in the Hall of Enlightenment, King Wen was likewise associated with him. For the receipt of an enfeoffed domain began with Hou Ji, while the accomplishment of the kingly enterprise was due to King Wen. Associating Hou Ji with Heaven served to honor Hou Ji and followed antiquity. Associating King Wen with the Supreme Lord served to express familial affection for King Wen and was instituted according to righteousness. Honoring those worthy of honor and loving one’s kin, each to the fullest extent: this is what made the forms of ritual complete, what moved the heart of Heaven, and what made the Zhou foremost among those who possessed the Way.

Spring and Autumn Annals

“The Duke of Zhou 州 went to Cao.” 〔Fifth year of Duke Huan.〕 “The duke met with the Duke of Zhou 周, the chief minister; the Marquis of Qi; the Master of Song; the Marquis of Wei; the Earl of Zheng; the Baron of Xu; and the Earl of Cao at Kuiqiu.” 〔Ninth year of Duke Xi.〕

Zhang Tianxian

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Instructor: “The passages set as the topic have clear explanations in the commentary, but writers generally fail to integrate them, producing tedious, fragmented work that wearies the reader. This composition fully grasps the commentary’s meaning, and its argument flows naturally and continuously. It has profoundly understood the teaching conveyed through connecting and comparing events.”

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Instructor: “Clear reasoning and vigorous language.”

Comment by Examiner Xu, Instructor: “Careful and rigorous.”

When a feudal lord used the rites of a court visit as a pretext, the Spring and Autumn Annals examined the designation used for him and recorded his original standing; when a chief minister participated in a meeting…

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
禮春秋隆所稱而正其分盖諸侯莫貴於稱公
而國宜常守宰臣莫貴於兼秩而分非常尊春
秋得不於州寔宰孔而兩致其意哉昔者河内
州寔度國多難棄彼郊畿之地躬脩如曹之禮
論其爵則諸侯也論其如則外事也春秋胡為
進秩稱公而又録其所往耶盖聞公也以賢入
相而以相出守是昔為師保之臣今居藩翰之
職無異乎衞武之入相于周畢髙之保釐東土
矣何乃履滿弗戒而圖國無良執德不恒而依
===
人是賴今日假禮於曹明日資餼於魯是固曹
之過賓而我之寓公也淳于城陽之墟豈州公
所有乎經故書公以隆其稱又書如曹者將有
其末先録其本為爵尊而居正之戒若夫周有
宰孔為王輔臣奉賜胙之命與葵丘之會其在
朝則冢卿也其出會則貴賓也春秋胡為加秩
書公而不殊會耶盖聞公也累官大宰而兼任
三公是上焉無乎師保而下焉行乎端揆無異
乎大禹之宅百揆周公之出正百工矣然
punctuated: 禮，春秋隆所稱而正其分。盖諸侯莫貴於稱公，而國宜常守；宰臣莫貴於兼秩，而分非常尊。春秋得不於州寔、宰孔而兩致其意哉？昔者河内州寔度國多難，棄彼郊畿之地，躬脩如曹之禮。論其爵，則諸侯也；論其如，則外事也。春秋胡為進秩稱公，而又録其所往耶？盖聞公也，以賢入相，而以相出守，是昔為師保之臣，今居藩翰之職，無異乎衞武之入相于周、畢髙之保釐東土矣。何乃履滿弗戒，而圖國無良；執德不恒，而依人是賴？今日假禮於曹，明日資餼於魯，是固曹之過賓，而我之寓公也。淳于城陽之墟，豈州公所有乎？經故書公以隆其稱，又書如曹者，將有其末，先録其本，為爵尊而居正之戒。若夫周有宰孔，為王輔臣，奉賜胙之命，與葵丘之會，其在朝則冢卿也，其出會則貴賓也。春秋胡為加秩書公，而不殊會耶？盖聞公也，累官大宰，而兼任三公，是上焉無乎師保，而下焉行乎端揆，無異乎大禹之宅百揆、周公之出正百工矣。然
translation_en:
…rites, the Spring and Autumn Annals elevates the designation used while setting right the distinctions of status. For the regional lords, no designation is more honorable than “duke,” yet they ought always to preserve their domains; for a chief minister, no honor is greater than holding concurrent ranks, yet his station does not invariably entitle him to precedence. Could the Spring and Autumn Annals fail to convey both these intentions in its treatment of Zhou Shi and Zai Kong?

Formerly, Zhou Shi of Henei, judging his state beset by troubles, abandoned that land near the royal capital and personally performed the courtesies of a visit to Cao. In rank, he was a regional lord; his visit was an affair beyond his borders. Why, then, does the Spring and Autumn Annals raise his rank by calling him “duke,” while also recording where he went? We have heard that this duke entered service as a minister because of his worthiness, and then left the court to govern a domain as a minister. Thus, formerly a royal preceptor or guardian, he now served as a bulwark of the realm. This was no different from Duke Wu of Wei entering ministerial service under Zhou, or Bi Gao protecting and governing the eastern lands. Why, then, did he occupy so exalted a position without caution and lack sound plans for his state, failing to remain constant in virtue and relying instead on others? Today he used ceremonial courtesy as a pretext to visit Cao; tomorrow he depended on provisions from Lu. He was indeed a passing guest in Cao and a displaced lord residing in our state. Did the old sites of Chunyu and Chengyang still belong to the Duke of Zhou? The Classic therefore writes “duke” to honor his designation, but also writes that he “went to Cao.” Before recording the eventual outcome, it first records its beginning, as an admonition that one who holds exalted rank must remain in his proper place.

As for Zai Kong of Zhou, he was a minister assisting the king. Bearing the command to bestow sacrificial meat, he attended the meeting at Kuiqiu. At court he was the chief minister; abroad at the meeting he was an honored guest. Why, then, does the Spring and Autumn Annals enhance his rank by writing “duke,” yet not distinguish his attendance from that of the others? We have heard that this duke rose through successive offices to become Grand Steward and concurrently held office among the Three Dukes. Thus, above, he had no position as preceptor or guardian [?], while below, he performed the duties of chief minister. This was no different from the Great Yu presiding over the various administrative offices, or the Duke of Zhou going forth to direct the hundred officials. Yet…

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
僭爵受祿則莫非王臣宅中居外皆侯于周服
分有均勞之義貴非常尊之比是宜諸侯莫先
而王人同序也儲君殊會之禮豈宰臣敢當乎
經故書宰兼公以隆其稱而不殊會者謹夫臣
禮正夫大分焉爵尊而居下之勸吁觀春秋尊
州寔而不沒其如曹則知尊爵可貴而君道難
觀春秋隆宰孔而不待以殊會則知尊爵可兼
而臣道卑書曰惟德是輔有國者明此必知所
難而保其尊易曰黃裳元吉相國者明此必知
===
所卑而永無咎如曹之事葵丘之會豈惟讀經
者所當知
公會齊侯宋公陳侯衞侯鄭伯許男曹伯
于鹹〔僖公十三年〕諸侯城緣陵〔僖公十四年〕
陳塤
同考試官教諭周 批 緣陵功罪所以異
於城邢封衞處學者多欠區别此作據經組傳
說盡齊桓得失如權衡稱物錙銖不爽殆知春
秋家法者
punctuated:
僭爵受祿，則莫非王臣；宅中居外，皆侯于周。服分有均勞之義，貴非常尊之比，是宜諸侯莫先，而王人同序也。儲君殊會之禮，豈宰臣敢當乎？經故書宰兼公，以隆其稱；而不殊會者，謹夫臣禮，正夫大分焉，爵尊而居下之勸。吁！觀春秋尊州寔而不沒其如曹，則知尊爵可貴而君道難；觀春秋隆宰孔而不待以殊會，則知尊爵可兼而臣道卑。書曰：「惟德是輔。」有國者明此，必知所難而保其尊。易曰：「黃裳元吉。」相國者明此，必知所卑而永無咎。如曹之事，葵丘之會，豈惟讀經者所當知？

公會齊侯、宋公、陳侯、衞侯、鄭伯、許男、曹伯于鹹〔僖公十三年〕。諸侯城緣陵〔僖公十四年〕。

陳塤

同考試官教諭周批：緣陵功罪所以異於城邢封衞處，學者多欠區别。此作據經組傳，說盡齊桓得失，如權衡稱物，錙銖不爽，殆知春秋家法者。
translation_en:
…though they usurp rank [?] and receive emoluments, they are all the king’s subjects; whether stationed at the center or residing outside it, all are lords subject to Zhou. Their duties and allotted stations entail sharing the burdens of service; their eminence is not comparable to permanently exalted status. It is therefore fitting that no regional lord should precede them, yet they should be listed in the same sequence as the king’s representatives. How could a chief minister presume to accept the ceremonial distinction accorded to the heir apparent by recording his participation in an assembly separately? Thus the Classic records both his office of chief minister and his title of duke, to exalt his designation. Yet by not recording his participation separately, it safeguards the propriety owed by a subject and rectifies the fundamental distinction between ruler and subject. This encourages those of exalted rank to remain in a subordinate position.

Ah! When we observe that the Spring and Autumn Annals honors Zhou Shi without suppressing his journey to Cao, we understand that exalted rank deserves esteem, but the way of a ruler is difficult. When we observe that the Spring and Autumn Annals elevates Zai Kong without granting him a separate record of participation in the assembly, we understand that exalted rank may be held concurrently with office, but the way of a subject requires humility. The Book of Documents says: “It is virtue alone that [Heaven] supports.” Rulers who understand this will surely recognize the difficulties of their position and preserve their exalted standing. The Book of Changes says: “A yellow lower garment: supreme good fortune.” Ministers assisting a state who understand this will surely recognize their subordinate position and remain forever free from blame. Are the journey to Cao and the assembly at Kuiqiu matters that only readers of the Classic ought to understand?

“The duke met with the marquis of Qi, the duke of Song, the marquis of Chen, the marquis of Wei, the earl of Zheng, the baron of Xu, and the earl of Cao at Xian.” 〔Thirteenth year of Duke Xi.〕 “The regional lords fortified Yuanling.” 〔Fourteenth year of Duke Xi.〕

Chen Xun.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Instructor: Students frequently fail to distinguish why the merits and faults of the affair at Yuanling differ from those involved in fortifying Xing and establishing Wei. This composition takes the Classic as its basis and weaves together the commentaries, fully explaining Duke Huan of Qi’s successes and failures. Like a balance weighing objects, it does not err by the smallest measure. Its author surely understands the interpretive principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals tradition.

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
考試官教諭姜批文有抑揚可嘉
考試官教諭徐批得貴王賤伯之旨
霸主恤小而失於專春秋異詞以譏其專此緣
陵之諸侯所以前目後凡而不序春秋貴王賤
霸之意見矣嘅昔蠢爾淮夷敢萌窺伺之志蕞
爾杞國日受侵逼之危經斯世者所宜慮也于
時齊桓主霸憂于厥心控大扶小首定于鹹之
議量功命日遂建緣陵之城徙其朝市于以去
危而即安移其人民于以就利而避害俾夏肄
===
之五廟不底于丘墟杞國之四民得免於塗炭
內安外攘桓之功可少哉常情觀此宜若深合
於城邢之恤患而遠邁乎楚丘之專封矣君子
則曰救急恤憐固為霸者之功築邑遷國必須
天子之命使桓於是時稟命於周室監之以王
卿則事功或半於他役而道義無歉於吾心雖
南仲之城朔方仲山甫之城東方不是過也夫
何築之登登齊築之也命不請於王朝往哉生
生齊遷之也事不聞於天子為力固勤事則專
punctuated:
考試官教諭姜批：文有抑揚，可嘉。
考試官教諭徐批：得貴王賤伯之旨。
霸主恤小而失於專，春秋異詞以譏其專。此緣陵之諸侯所以前目後凡而不序，春秋貴王賤霸之意見矣。嘅昔蠢爾淮夷，敢萌窺伺之志；蕞爾杞國，日受侵逼之危，經斯世者所宜慮也。于時齊桓主霸，憂于厥心，控大扶小，首定于鹹之議；量功命日，遂建緣陵之城。徙其朝市，于以去危而即安；移其人民，于以就利而避害。俾夏肄之五廟不底于丘墟，杞國之四民得免於塗炭。內安外攘，桓之功可少哉？常情觀此，宜若深合於城邢之恤患，而遠邁乎楚丘之專封矣。君子則曰：救急恤憐，固為霸者之功；築邑遷國，必須天子之命。使桓於是時稟命於周室，監之以王卿，則事功或半於他役，而道義無歉於吾心。雖南仲之城朔方、仲山甫之城東方，不是過也。夫何築之登登，齊築之也，命不請於王朝；往哉生生，齊遷之也，事不聞於天子。為力固勤，事則專
translation_en:
Examiner Jiang, Instructor, comments: The writing is commendable for its measured praise and censure.

Examiner Xu, Instructor, comments: It grasps the principle of honoring the king and lowering the hegemon.

The hegemon cared for a small state but erred in acting on his own authority. The Spring and Autumn Annals varies its wording to criticize that presumption. This is why the lords involved at Yuanling are individually named in the earlier entry but collectively designated, without an ordered listing, in the later one. Here the Annals’ intention to honor the king and lower the hegemon becomes apparent.

Alas, in those days the unruly Huai Yi dared harbor designs of aggression, while the tiny state of Qi 杞 daily faced the danger of encroachment. Those responsible for governing the age ought to have been concerned. At that time Duke Huan of Qi 齊 held the hegemony and took this concern to heart. Restraining the great and supporting the small, he first settled the deliberations at Xian; then, assessing the labor and appointing a date, he built the walls of Yuanling. He transferred the court and markets of Qi 杞, bringing them from danger to security, and relocated its people so that they might gain advantages and avoid harm. Thus the five ancestral temples of the surviving line of Xia did not fall into ruins, and the four classes of people in Qi 杞 escaped misery. Securing peace within and repelling threats from without—could Duke Huan’s achievement be considered slight? Viewed in ordinary terms, this would seem fully consonant with the relief of distress shown in walling Xing, and far superior to the unauthorized establishment of a state at Chuqiu.

The gentleman, however, says: Relieving emergencies and caring for the distressed are indeed achievements of a hegemon; but building a town and relocating a state necessarily require the Son of Heaven’s command. Had Duke Huan at that time sought orders from the Zhou royal house and placed the undertaking under the supervision of a royal minister, his practical achievement might have been half that of other undertakings, yet in morality and righteousness he would have left my heart nothing to regret. Even Nan Zhong’s walling of Shuofang and Zhong Shanfu’s walling in the east would not have surpassed it.

Why, then, as the walls rose with resounding blows, was it Qi 齊 that built them, without requesting a command from the royal court? And as the people went forth to live anew [?], was it Qi 齊 that relocated them, without reporting the matter to the Son of Heaven? The effort was certainly diligent, but the undertaking was presumptuous …

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
矣方諸邢之自遷而從拳救急者豈可同日語
乎比於衛之旣滅而擅拳專封者其罪薄乎云
耳春秋正義不謀利明道不計功故雖列序會
鹹之八國而終凡舉緣陵之諸侯旣異於城邢
之再序三師亦異於楚丘之深沒其迹貴王賤
霸以正待人之體何如哉雖然桓之城緣陵以
遷杞固可罪矣觀其會首止以定王儲盟葵丘
而明王禁于洮之靖難甯母之通貢桓於周室
有大功焉是則以道義言固三王之罪人以功
===
烈言亦五霸之巨擘論者謂春秋明王法而不
廢五霸之功信夫
禮記
是故君子不自大其事不自尚其功以求
處情過行弗率以求處厚彰人之善而美
人之功以求下賢
鄭伯和
同考試官敎諭方批辭約意盡作長題
難得如此殆經生中之穎出者宜取爲本房冠
punctuated:
矣。方諸邢之自遷而從拳救急者，豈可同日語乎？比於衛之旣滅而擅拳專封者，其罪薄乎云耳。《春秋》正義不謀利，明道不計功，故雖列序會鹹之八國，而終凡舉緣陵之諸侯。旣異於城邢之再序三師，亦異於楚丘之深沒其迹。貴王賤霸，以正待人之體何如哉！雖然，桓之城緣陵以遷杞，固可罪矣。觀其會首止以定王儲，盟葵丘而明王禁，于洮之靖難、甯母之通貢，桓於周室有大功焉。是則以道義言，固三王之罪人；以功烈言，亦五霸之巨擘。論者謂《春秋》明王法而不廢五霸之功，信夫！

《禮記》
是故君子不自大其事，不自尚其功，以求處情；過行弗率，以求處厚；彰人之善，而美人之功，以求下賢。
鄭伯和

同考試官敎諭方批：辭約意盡，作長題難得如此，殆經生中之穎出者，宜取爲本房冠。
translation_en:
…indeed. How could this be spoken of in the same breath as Xing’s relocation on its own initiative, when he acted expediently [?] to relieve an emergency? Compared with his arrogating authority [?] and independently enfeoffing a ruler after Wei had already been destroyed, one can only say that his offense was lighter. The Spring and Autumn Annals upholds righteousness without seeking advantage and makes the Way clear without reckoning achievements. Thus, although it lists individually the eight states that met at Xian, it ultimately refers collectively to the feudal lords at Yuanling. This differs both from its listing the three armies a second time in recording the walling of Xing and from its thoroughly concealing the participants’ traces in the case of Chuqiu. How admirable is its principle of honoring kingship and depreciating hegemony, judging men by what is right!

Nevertheless, Duke Huan can certainly be blamed for walling Yuanling to relocate Qi 杞. Yet consider his meeting at Shouzhi to secure the royal heir, his covenant at Kuiqiu to make the royal prohibitions clear, his pacification of the troubles at Tao, and his arrangements for tribute at Ningmu: Huan rendered great service to the royal house of Zhou. Thus, judged by the Way and righteousness, he was certainly an offender against the Three Kings; judged by his achievements, he was also an outstanding figure among the Five Hegemons. Those who discuss the matter say that the Spring and Autumn Annals elucidates royal law without discounting the achievements of the Five Hegemons. How true!

Book of Rites
“Therefore the gentleman does not magnify his own deeds or exalt his own achievements, seeking thereby to remain true to the actual circumstances. He does not follow excessive conduct, seeking thereby to abide in substantial virtue. He makes others’ goodness manifest and praises their achievements, seeking thereby to place himself below the worthy.”
Zheng Bohe 鄭伯和

Comment by Associate Examiner Fang, Instructor: “The wording is concise and the meaning fully expressed. In an essay on a long topic, such a result is rare. He is surely outstanding among students of the Classics and should be ranked first in this examining section.”

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
考試官教諭姜批寫出自卑尊人意
思宛然在目
考試官教諭徐批詞不違理可錄
記者歷言君子謙己而尊人無非自卑之道也
蓋人莫難於自卑也使或矜於己而加於人則
豈為君子之道哉記表記者因言謚以尊名節
以一惠而及於此謂夫君子恭儉以求役仁而
處己也謙信讓以求役禮而與人也敬是故事
雖為人所大己未嘗自以為大功雖為人所尚
===
己未嘗自以為高所以然者豈沽名哉蓋欲求
以處乎情實之地不肯虛為矯飾也行或過高
而苟難則不敢率之於身事或驚世而駭俗則
不敢措之於己所以然者豈飾詐哉蓋欲求以
處乎篤厚之道不欲過為已甚也至若人或有
善己則彰而明之人或有功己則頌而美之其
為是者非虛譽也惟欲求以下乎有善之人而
不沒其善也求以下乎有功之人而不掩其功
也又豈敢媚嫉而蔽賢哉是則曰處情曰處厚
punctuated:
考試官教諭姜批：寫出自卑尊人意思，宛然在目。
考試官教諭徐批：詞不違理，可錄。
記者歷言君子謙己而尊人，無非自卑之道也。蓋人莫難於自卑也，使或矜於己而加於人，則豈為君子之道哉？記《表記》者因言謚以尊名，節以一惠，而及於此，謂夫君子恭儉以求役仁，而處己也謙；信讓以求役禮，而與人也敬。是故事雖為人所大，己未嘗自以為大；功雖為人所尚，己未嘗自以為高。所以然者，豈沽名哉？蓋欲求以處乎情實之地，不肯虛為矯飾也。行或過高而苟難，則不敢率之於身；事或驚世而駭俗，則不敢措之於己。所以然者，豈飾詐哉？蓋欲求以處乎篤厚之道，不欲過為已甚也。至若人或有善，己則彰而明之；人或有功，己則頌而美之。其為是者，非虛譽也，惟欲求以下乎有善之人而不沒其善也，求以下乎有功之人而不掩其功也。又豈敢媚嫉而蔽賢哉？是則曰處情，曰處厚
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Jiang, Instructor: The idea of humbling oneself and honoring others is brought vividly before the eyes.
Comment by Examiner Xu, Instructor: The wording does not depart from principle; it merits inclusion.
The compiler of the Record explains in succession how the gentleman humbles himself and honors others: all of this concerns the way of lowering oneself. Indeed, nothing is harder for people than lowering themselves. If someone boasts of himself and sets himself above others, how could this be the gentleman’s way? In discussing how posthumous titles honor a person’s name while being confined to a single excellence, the compiler of “The Record of Exemplary Conduct” in the Book of Rites proceeds to this point. He means that the gentleman seeks to serve benevolence through reverence and frugality, and is humble in his conduct toward himself; he seeks to serve ritual propriety through trustworthiness and deference, and is respectful in his dealings with others. Thus, although others regard his deeds as great, he never regards them as great himself; although others esteem his achievements, he never considers himself exalted on their account. Is he acting this way to purchase a reputation? He seeks, rather, to ground himself in genuine feeling and reality, refusing empty pretense and embellishment. If a course of conduct is excessively lofty and difficult merely for difficulty’s sake, he dares not adopt it himself; if an undertaking would startle the world and shock customary sensibilities, he dares not take it upon himself. Is he acting this way to cloak deceit? He seeks to abide by the way of sincerity and generosity, unwilling to go to extremes. As for others, if they possess goodness, he makes it manifest and brings it to light; if they have achievements, he praises and commends them. In doing this, he is not offering empty praise. He wishes only to place himself below those who possess goodness, without effacing their goodness, and below those who have achievements, without concealing their achievements. How, then, could he dare to flatter or envy [?] and obscure the worthy? Thus, the expressions “abiding in genuine feeling” and “abiding in generosity”…

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
無非所以謙於己曰彰善曰美功無非所以尊
乎人君子自卑之道何其至哉大抵此章爲人
臣言也考之上章有曰舜禹文王周公有君民
之大德有事君之小心下文又曰后稷之爲烈
也欲行之浮於名也自謂便人合而觀之于以
見人臣之道以仁爲本雖有庇民之大德不敢
有君民之心必卑己而尊人小心而畏義然後
可以盡其道也故惟舜禹文王周公可以爲仁
之厚而后稷則庶乎近之舍是而欲他求也幾
===
希矣
故孝弟忠順之行立而後可以爲人
洪晅
同考試官教諭方 批 說理詳明是亦能
盡人道者
考試官教諭姜 批 敷腴
考試官教諭徐 批 文有矩度
惟能備夫成人之行斯不愧於爲人矣盖冠所
以責成人之行也誠能備其行而不虧則人道
punctuated:
無非所以謙於己；曰彰善，曰美功，無非所以尊乎人。君子自卑之道，何其至哉！大抵此章爲人臣言也。考之上章，有曰：「舜禹文王周公，有君民之大德，有事君之小心。」下文又曰：「后稷之爲烈也，欲行之浮於名也，自謂便人。」合而觀之，于以見人臣之道，以仁爲本。雖有庇民之大德，不敢有君民之心，必卑己而尊人，小心而畏義，然後可以盡其道也。故惟舜禹文王周公，可以爲仁之厚，而后稷則庶乎近之。舍是而欲他求也，幾希矣！

故孝弟忠順之行立而後可以爲人。
洪晅
同考試官教諭方批：說理詳明，是亦能盡人道者。
考試官教諭姜批：敷腴。
考試官教諭徐批：文有矩度。

惟能備夫成人之行，斯不愧於爲人矣。盖冠所以責成人之行也，誠能備其行而不虧，則人道
translation_en:
…all are means of being humble oneself. Manifesting others’ goodness and praising their achievements are all means of honoring others. How consummate is the gentleman’s way of humbling himself! Broadly speaking, this chapter addresses those who serve as ministers. Examining the preceding chapter, we find: “Shun, Yu, King Wen, and the Duke of Zhou possessed the great virtue required to rule the people, yet maintained the cautious heart required to serve a ruler.” The text below also says: “As for Hou Ji’s achievements, he wished his conduct to exceed his reputation and called himself merely an ordinary man.” Taken together, these passages show that benevolence is the foundation of the minister’s way. Even possessing the great virtue needed to shelter the people, he dares not harbor the intention of ruling them. He must humble himself and honor others, remain cautious, and hold righteousness in awe; only then can he fully fulfill his way. Thus only Shun, Yu, King Wen, and the Duke of Zhou may be regarded as possessing profound benevolence, while Hou Ji came close to it. To abandon this and seek elsewhere would offer scant hope indeed!

“Thus, only after conduct marked by filial devotion, fraternal respect, loyalty, and obedience has been established can one be a person.”
By Hong Xuan.
Associate Examiner Fang, Instructor, comments: “The reasoning is detailed and clear. This, too, is someone capable of fully fulfilling the human way.”
Examiner Jiang, Instructor, comments: “Ample and rich.”
Examiner Xu, Instructor, comments: “The writing observes proper standards.”

Only by possessing the full conduct of an adult can one be worthy of being a person. For the capping ceremony is the means of demanding adult conduct. If one can truly fulfill that conduct without deficiency, then the human way…

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
盡矣尚何愧於爲人乎記冠義者謂夫備人道
者必本於禮責成人者必始於冠彼人之冠也
以内言之則有父焉有兄焉事父兄而不盡其
禮則衣裳而禽犢矣可乎以外言之則有君焉
有長焉事君長而不盡其禮則冠冕而夷裔矣
得乎是故入而處於家也必温清定省承顏順
志而於事親盡其孝敬恭友愛克念天顯而於
事兄盡其弟如是則孝弟之行立矣出而處於
外也必攄忠納悃恪共厥職而於事君盡其忠
===
徐行後長謙卑退遜而於事長盡其順如是則
忠順之行立矣夫成人之行既立則成人之禮
以備由是父焉安其孝而可以爲之子兄焉安
其弟而可以爲之弟爲子爲弟之道夫豈有不
盡者哉君焉安其忠而可以爲之臣長焉安其
順而可以爲之少爲臣爲少之道抑何有不盡
者哉夫然則人之成也以行爲之先而行之立
也以禮爲之要冠禮之責成人也可不重歟嗟
夫冠者禮之始也嘉事之重者也先王知其然
punctuated: 盡矣，尚何愧於爲人乎？記冠義者謂夫備人道者必本於禮，責成人者必始於冠。彼人之冠也，以内言之，則有父焉，有兄焉；事父兄而不盡其禮，則衣裳而禽犢矣，可乎？以外言之，則有君焉，有長焉；事君長而不盡其禮，則冠冕而夷裔矣，得乎？是故入而處於家也，必温清定省，承顏順志，而於事親盡其孝；敬恭友愛，克念天顯，而於事兄盡其弟。如是則孝弟之行立矣。出而處於外也，必攄忠納悃，恪共厥職，而於事君盡其忠；徐行後長，謙卑退遜，而於事長盡其順。如是則忠順之行立矣。夫成人之行既立，則成人之禮以備。由是父焉安其孝，而可以爲之子；兄焉安其弟，而可以爲之弟。爲子爲弟之道，夫豈有不盡者哉？君焉安其忠，而可以爲之臣；長焉安其順，而可以爲之少。爲臣爲少之道，抑何有不盡者哉？夫然則人之成也，以行爲之先；而行之立也，以禮爲之要。冠禮之責成人也，可不重歟？嗟夫！冠者，禮之始也，嘉事之重者也。先王知其然
translation_en:
…are fully fulfilled. What cause, then, remains for shame at being human? The author of “The Meaning of the Capping Ceremony” says that fulfilling the human way must be grounded in ritual propriety, and that requiring a person to assume adult responsibilities must begin with capping. Consider the person being capped: within the household, he has a father and elder brothers. If he serves them without fully observing the requisite proprieties, he is merely a bird or calf [?] dressed in human clothing. Can this be acceptable? Outside the household, he has a ruler and elders. If he serves them without fully observing the requisite proprieties, he is merely a barbarian wearing a ceremonial cap. Can this be right?

Thus, when at home, he must keep his parents warm in winter and cool in summer [?], settle them at night and inquire after them in the morning, attend upon them and comply with their wishes, thereby fulfilling his filial duty in serving them. He must be respectful, reverent, affectionate, and loving, ever mindful of the manifest bonds ordained by Heaven, thereby fulfilling his fraternal duty in serving his elder brothers. In this way, filial and fraternal conduct is established. When outside the household, he must express his loyalty, offer his sincerity, and reverently discharge his duties, thereby fulfilling his loyalty in serving his ruler. He must walk slowly behind his elders, be humble and yielding, and defer to others, thereby fulfilling his obedience in serving his elders. In this way, loyal and obedient conduct is established.

Once adult conduct is established, the ritual requirements of adulthood are fulfilled. His father can then rest content in his filial devotion, and he is fit to be his son; his elder brothers can rest content in his fraternal respect, and he is fit to be their younger brother. How could any part of the duties of a son or younger brother remain unfulfilled? His ruler can rest content in his loyalty, and he is fit to be his subject; his elders can rest content in his obedience, and he is fit to be their junior. How could any part of the duties of a subject or junior remain unfulfilled?

Thus, in attaining adulthood, conduct comes first; and in establishing conduct, ritual propriety is essential. Can the capping ceremony’s demand that one assume adult responsibilities be treated lightly? Ah! Capping is the beginning of ritual observance and a weighty auspicious occasion. The former kings understood this…

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
故行之於廟以示其尊筮日筮賓以致其敬何
也盖以孝弟忠順之行立而後孝弟忠順之化
行修巳治人之道胥此焉出先王所以重禮以
爲國本焉是故也後世禮教不備一切放廢而
於冠之一事尤爲率略是以人道不明出治無
本而於天下之禮卒不可行也噫
第貳塲
論
孔子與天地參而四時同
同考試官訓導俞批官様題目作者不
泛則畧惟此篇有源委有操縱詞健而豐氣雄
而正寫出孔子同造化之旨無餘是宜錄出
同考試官教諭魏批是論說孔子道德
教化詞約義該宛然一太極在目精微之學昌
大之氣率於此發之春闈大捷又當爲子預占
考試官教諭姜批周子之學在太極
一圖而通書所以發其蘊也此作根本圖說而
banxin: 鄉試錄 四十七 張燮
punctuated:
故行之於廟，以示其尊；筮日筮賓，以致其敬。何也？盖以孝弟忠順之行立，而後孝弟忠順之化行，修巳治人之道胥此焉出。先王所以重禮以爲國本焉，是故也。後世禮教不備，一切放廢，而於冠之一事尤爲率略。是以人道不明，出治無本，而於天下之禮卒不可行也。噫！

第貳塲
論
孔子與天地參而四時同

同考試官訓導俞批：官様題目，作者不泛則畧。惟此篇有源委，有操縱，詞健而豐，氣雄而正，寫出孔子同造化之旨無餘，是宜錄出。

同考試官教諭魏批：是論說孔子道德教化，詞約義該，宛然一太極在目。精微之學，昌大之氣，率於此發之。春闈大捷，又當爲子預占。

考試官教諭姜批：周子之學在太極一圖，而通書所以發其蘊也。此作根本圖說而
translation_en:
…Thus they performed it in the ancestral temple to show its dignity, and used milfoil divination to select the day and the guest, thereby expressing their reverence. Why was this? Only after conduct marked by filial piety, fraternal deference, loyalty, and obedience is established can moral transformation through these virtues spread. The way of cultivating oneself and governing others proceeds entirely from this. This is why the former kings esteemed ritual as the foundation of the state. In later ages, ritual instruction became deficient, and everything was neglected and abandoned; the capping ceremony in particular was treated perfunctorily. Consequently, the human way became obscured, governance lacked a foundation, and the rites of the realm ultimately could not be put into practice. Alas!

Second Session
Discourse
Confucius Forms a Triad with Heaven and Earth and Is in Harmony with the Four Seasons

Comment by Associate Examiner Yu, Assistant Instructor: With a conventional examination topic of this kind, writers tend to be either vague or cursory. This essay alone traces the matter from its source to its ramifications and handles it with freedom and control. Its language is vigorous and rich, its spirit powerful and upright. It fully expresses the meaning of Confucius’s unity with the creative transformations of Heaven and Earth. It deserves to be selected for inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wei, Instructor: This discourse explains Confucius’s Way, virtue, and transforming instruction. Its language is concise and its meaning comprehensive: it is as though the Supreme Ultimate itself were before one’s eyes. Subtle and profound learning and a vast, flourishing spirit find full expression here. I would also venture to predict your great success in the spring Metropolitan Examination.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Instructor: Master Zhou’s learning is contained in the single Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate, while his Penetrating the Changes (Tongshu) unfolds its hidden meanings. This composition takes the Explanation of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate as its foundation and…

title: 弘治十四年福建鄉試錄
text:
加粧點而文理粲然蓋嘗究心理學者入闀之
秀無踰子矣
考試官教諭徐批文以理為主而能
輔之以氣斯為作家此論詞氣超邁所謂使人
擊節歎賞未如使人肅然生敬者也宜録之以
礪後進
論曰以太極之全體而擬聖人善言聖人者也
夫莫大於天地天地太極之體也莫久於四時
四時太極之用也聖人合陰陽之動靜妙五行
===
之生成道之高也配乎天德之厚也配乎地教
化之無窮也配乎四時故以一人之身位乎天
高地下之間而不見其小合乎四時變通之運
而不見其近非聖人全體太極其何以參天地
而同四時如此哉周子以是擬之可謂善言聖
人者矣請暢厥旨世之言聖人者多矣仰宫墻
之高廣窺堂室之深奥有以日月而擬道之高
者矣有以淵泉而擬德之厚者矣有以時雨而
擬教化之妙者矣殊不知日月天之一象耳未
punctuated:
加粧點，而文理粲然，蓋嘗究心理學者。入闀之秀，無踰子矣。

考試官教諭徐批：文以理為主，而能輔之以氣，斯為作家。此論詞氣超邁，所謂使人擊節歎賞，未如使人肅然生敬者也。宜録之，以礪後進。

論曰：以太極之全體而擬聖人，善言聖人者也。夫莫大於天地，天地，太極之體也；莫久於四時，四時，太極之用也。聖人合陰陽之動靜，妙五行之生成，道之高也配乎天，德之厚也配乎地，教化之無窮也配乎四時。故以一人之身，位乎天高地下之間，而不見其小；合乎四時變通之運，而不見其近。非聖人全體太極，其何以參天地而同四時如此哉？周子以是擬之，可謂善言聖人者矣。請暢厥旨。世之言聖人者多矣，仰宫墻之高廣，窺堂室之深奥，有以日月而擬道之高者矣，有以淵泉而擬德之厚者矣，有以時雨而擬教化之妙者矣。殊不知日月，天之一象耳，未
translation_en:
…adds embellishment, making the composition’s pattern and reasoning shine forth. The author has evidently devoted himself to the study of principle. Among the outstanding candidates entering the examination precinct [?], none surpasses you.

Comment by Examiner Xu, Instructor: Writing takes principle as its foundation; when the author can support it with vital force, he is a true master of composition. This discourse is surpassingly lofty in its language and spirit. As the saying goes, making readers beat time in admiration is less than making them feel solemn reverence. It should be recorded to spur on younger scholars.

The discourse reads: To compare the sage to the Supreme Ultimate in its entirety is to speak well of the sage.
